drivingQuestion: Who may bear an honorific title — why only three patriarchs and four matriarchs, and may slaves be called ׳father so-and-so׳?
outcomeNote: Both difficulties — the reason for restricting ׳patriarchs׳ and the apparent contradiction from Rabban Gamliel's household — are answered.

segments.he: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין קוֹרִין ״אָבוֹת״ אֶלָּא לִשְׁלֹשָׁה, וְאֵין קוֹרִין ״אִמָּהוֹת״ אֶלָּא לְאַרְבַּע.
segments.en: «The Sages taught» in a baraita: «One may only call three» people «patriarchs,» Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but not Jacob’s children. «And one may only call four» people «matriarchs,» Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, and Leah.

segments.he: אָבוֹת מַאי טַעְמָא? אִילֵּימָא מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא יָדְעִינַן אִי מֵרְאוּבֵן קָא אָתֵינַן אִי מִשִּׁמְעוֹן קָא אָתֵינַן, אִי הָכִי אִמָּהוֹת נָמֵי לָא יָדְעִינַן אִי מֵרָחֵל קָא אָתֵינַן אִי מִלֵּאָה קָא אָתֵינַן! אֶלָּא, עַד הָכָא חֲשִׁיבִי, טְפִי לָא חֲשִׁיבִי.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «What is the reason» for this exclusivity with regard to the «Patriarchs? If you say» that it is «because we do not know whether we descend from Reuben or from Simon,» so we cannot accurately say our father Reuben, for example, «if so,» with regard to the Matriarchs as well, «we do not know whether we descend from Rachel or from Leah,» and we should not call Rachel and Leah matriarchs either. «Instead,» the reason the sons of Jacob are not called patriarchs is not for that reason, but because «until» Jacob «they are significant» enough to be referred to as patriarchs, but «beyond» Jacob, «they are not significant» enough to be referred to as patriarchs.

segments.he: תַּנְיָא אִידָךְ: עֲבָדִים וּשְׁפָחוֹת אֵין קוֹרִין אוֹתָם ״אַבָּא פְּלוֹנִי״ וְ״אִמָּא פְּלוֹנִית״. וְשֶׁל רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הָיוּ קוֹרִים אוֹתָם ״אַבָּא פְּלוֹנִי״ וְ״אִמָּא פְּלוֹנִית״.
segments.en: This serves as an introduction; although older people are often referred to with the honorific: Father so-and-so, «it was taught in another» baraita: «One may not refer to slaves and maidservants as father [abba] so-and-so or mother [imma] so-and-so. But they would call» the slaves and maidservants «of Rabban Gamliel “father so-and-so” and “mother so-and-so.”»

The Gemara asks: Is a «story» cited in order «to contradict» the previously stated halakha? The Gemara answers: There is no contradiction; rather, «because» Rabban Gamliel’s servants «were significant,» they were addressed with these honorifics.

moves.summary: A baraita restricting the titles ׳patriarchs׳ and ׳matriarchs׳ to three and four
moves.about: a baraita that only three are called patriarchs and only four matriarchs

moves.summary: Why is the title ׳patriarchs׳ restricted to three?
moves.about: why the title ׳patriarchs׳ is restricted to three and withheld from the sons of Jacob

moves.cueHe: אילימא משום דלא ידעינן אי מראובן קא אתינן
moves.summary: Floats the candidate reason: we do not know from which of Jacob's sons we descend
moves.about: whether the reason is that we do not know from which of Jacob's sons we descend — rejected, since we equally do not know whether we descend from Rachel or Leah, yet both are called matriarchs

moves.summary: Knocks the candidate down: the same doubt applies to Rachel and Leah, who are called matriarchs
moves.about: the title stops at Jacob because up to him they are significant enough to be called patriarchs and beyond him they are not

moves.cueHe: אלא, עד הכא חשיבי, טפי לא חשיבי
moves.summary: The surviving answer: significance, not doubt of descent, sets the limit at Jacob
A second baraita: slaves are not called ׳father so-and-so׳, but Rabban Gamliel's were
moves.about: a baraita that slaves and maidservants are not called ׳father so-and-so׳ or ׳mother so-and-so׳, though Rabban Gamliel's were

moves.summary: Is a story brought to contradict the rule just taught?
moves.about: whether the baraita's own report of Rabban Gamliel's household may be adduced against the rule it has just stated

moves.summary: No contradiction: those slaves were themselves distinguished
moves.about: there is no contradiction: Rabban Gamliel's slaves were addressed with honorifics because they were of distinguished stature
